description: We are Super into Astronomy and would like to discover new astronomical objects. Looking for team members with UX Design skills and ability to Complile Big Data
summary: AstroTracker is a free, public web tool for watching the sky change in real NASA SPHEREx infrared images. Enter a sky position, an object name, or a comet or asteroid, and the app gathers every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from the indexed releases. It aligns them north-up and plays them as a short movie, blinks or subtracts two dates, or shows a motion trail. This makes asteroids, comets and fast-moving nearby stars stand out. Built on the open-source SkyDiff viewer, AstroTracker adds data reliability: a coverage chart by date and detector, clear messages that separate “no data” from “couldn’t confirm”, an image-quality inspector, and comparisons that only pair images taken at matching wavelengths. An AI helper, Ask SpaceLapse, explains what you’re seeing and how to use the app, and never claims a discovery. Image processing runs in your browser, streaming only the pixels it needs from NASA/IPAC’s public SPHEREx archive, with caching for fast revisits. Built-in checks run on the five challenge targets, including Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855 and Epsilon Indi B. Students and citizen scientists can explore the data and flag candidates for experts to check.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

  • Search: users search by coordinates, name or a moving object, and the app finds every matching SPHEREx exposure in a pre-built sky index.
  • Reading images: it downloads only the needed slice of each image from NASA’s public S3 archive, then aligns the frames on a common grid.
  • Views: time-lapse, blink, difference, motion trail and a deep stack, plus spectra and light curves.
  • Coverage panel: shows dates by detector and release, with clear “no data” vs “couldn’t confirm” messages.
  • Sharing: shareable links let others open the exact same view.

Benefits

  • No install, account or cost.
  • Fast: revisiting a view downloads nothing.
  • Honest about data gaps and quality flags.
  • Works on phones.
  • Links can be embedded in other sites.

Intended impact

To let students, amateurs and citizen scientists join the search for asteroids, comets and brown dwarfs in SPHEREx data. Previously, finds like these needed specialist software.

Tools, languages, hardware/software

  • Languages: JavaScript (browser), HTML/CSS and Python.
    • NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1/QR2/QR3, public S3),
    • CDS Sesame,
    • JPL Horizons,
    • IMCCE Miriade/SkyBoT
    • Gaia DR3
    • OpenAI GPT-5, with an optional OpenRouter backup.
    • Libraries: astropy, NumPy, Flask, and jsdom for testing.
  • Development: GitHub with GitHub Actions (tests, weekly index rebuild), Vercel hosting, standard laptops, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.
  • Credit: leverages open-source SPHEREx Time-Lapse project, for its data-handling techniques.

How is it creative?

  • It turns a 102-band infrared survey into a simple “spot what moved” movie.
  • It reads only the bytes needed from large archive files.
  • It keeps “no data” separate from “couldn’t confirm”.
  • It aligns frames on a moving comet so the comet stays still while stars stream past.

Factors considered

  • Data reliability: multiple releases, outages, partial failures and superseded QR2 data.
  • Scientific caution: no discovery claims, caveats for each view, and checks that wavelengths match.
  • Speed and bandwidth, and keeping the index current with a weekly rebuild.
  • Accessibility and phone use.
  • AI safety and cost: rate limits, a daily cap, a backup model and keys kept on the server.
  • Testing: 306 automated tests (92 Python, 214 JavaScript), 100% of JavaScript lines covered, plus checks against NASA’s archive.
  • Near-zero-cost hosting: the only running cost is the AI helper, which has a spending cap.

How did we check that the app works as expected?

1. Against NASA’s own archive

  • Hand checks: we checked Barnard’s Star and WISE 0855 against NASA’s DR1 and QR3 records: dates, image counts per detector, coverage and missing releases. These are written up in docs/VERIFICATION.md.
  • Scripts: these repeat the release and target checks, and measure how the app recovers from failed downloads.
  • Duplicates: we confirmed each duplicated image resolves to the newest release.

2. Inside the app

  • Run five target checks:
    • finds coverage live
    • builds real cutouts from the earliest, middle and latest visits
    • confirms quality and wavelength data load
    • runs a test comparison

Even when everything passes, it still says “inspect manually”.

  • Seeing it with your own eyes: in blink mode, Barnard’s Star visibly shifts in the expected direction, which shows positions and alignment are right.

3. Automated tests

  • 306 tests in total: 214 JavaScript tests (100% of lines, 96.6% of branches) and 92 Python tests. They run on every push.
    • releases and duplicates
    • empty, partial and unreachable archives
    • unreachable moving-object searches
    • the coverage chart
    • the cache
    • the five target checks
    • the assistant
    • repo links
    • full-page tests in a simulated browser
  • Written from requirements: tests encode what the app should do, not what it already did. Several failed at first and exposed real bugs, which we fixed.
  • Sabotage checks: we broke key features on purpose and confirmed the tests caught it.

4. By hand on the live site

  • Desktop and phone layouts, keyboard use and focus.
  • Assistant, live: correct answers, and correct rejection of bad requests and rate-limit breaches. Testing caught a science error in its instructions, which we fixed.

Gaps to state openly:

  • Only two targets were checked in depth.
  • Most tests use recorded NASA responses rather than live ones.
  • Test failures are reported but don’t block changes.
  • There’s no automatic comparison of measured motion against Gaia yet.
  • The backup AI model hasn’t been tried with a real key.

How is our project different from SkyDiff?

SpaceLapse is built on SkyDiff (github.com/ShivenKhurana1/skydiff, previously spherex-timelapse), an open-source browser viewer for SPHEREx. SkyDiff provided the engine:

  • the sky index of about 1.2 million images
  • downloading only part of each file from NASA’s S3 bucket
  • alignment and bad-pixel masking
  • time-lapse, blink, difference, motion trail and deep stack views
  • following moving objects, asteroid labels and Scan for changes
  • light curves, spectra and the Report button

What we added, by category:

Trustworthy data

1. The newest NASA release (DR1): the index builder now includes the DR1 release alongside QR2 and QR3. When the same image appears in more than one release, the app shows it once and picks the newest processing, so old QR2 copies drop out.

2. “No data” vs “couldn’t confirm”: if part of the archive index fails to load, the app uses what it got and warns you. If it all fails, it says coverage is unknown. It never shows a failure as an empty sky.

3. Archive coverage chart: shows which dates and detectors have images. Tap a mark to jump to that date.

4. Archive releases & freshness: shows which releases are indexed, how many images, and when the index was last updated. It warns that an image covering the target doesn’t guarantee the target can be seen in it.

5. Inspect image quality & source files: for each frame, shows which quality problems NASA flagged, with an optional overlay on the image and links to the original files.

6. Stricter rules for measurements: brightness plots and spectra use only fully clean pixels, stricter than the rules for display.

Safer comparisons

7. Compare two dates (A/B residual mode): a sixth view that subtracts one chosen date from another.

8. Wavelength window: keep only images taken within a chosen wavelength range.

9. Comparisons refuse rather than mislead: they’re blocked when the two images’ wavelengths or quality data don’t match, with an explanation.

10. Caveats for each view: each view explains what it can and can’t show, for example that motion trails are exploratory.

11. Reset when the wavelength changes: changing the wavelength clears old date picks and scan results, so stale comparisons aren’t misread.

Challenge tools

12. Five challenge targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis, each with a guide and an honest note about its position (for example, that WISE 0855 has moved about 2′ from its catalogue marker).

13. Run five target checks: one button checks real images for all five targets, with a cancel option and an export of the results.

14. Catalogue context: optional Gaia DR3 or AllWISE star markers on the image, from VizieR, to tell known stars from anything new.

Easier to use

15. Ask SpaceLapse: an AI helper that answers “what am I looking at?” and “how do I…?” questions. It uses a summary of the current screen data (for astrophysics-typed questions), and utilizes UI selector and readme/docs for app-guide questions. Note, the app defers to human judgment and never claims a discovery.

16. New landing page:

  • a “Can you spot what moved?” before-and-after demo (simulated, and labelled as such)
  • featured destinations
  • a “Choose. Play. Compare.” walkthrough
  • an explainer of where the images come from

17. Full screen with its own play, previous and next buttons, plus a fit-image option.

18. Phones and accessibility: mobile layout, keyboard use, screen-reader labels and visible focus rings.

19. Faster revisits: images you’ve already loaded are kept in memory (up to 150 MB), and frames share header downloads.

20. Copy view link, plus export observation (JSON) with the target, releases, settings and index date, and export candidates (CSV) from a scan.

Behind the scenes

21. Ask SpaceLapse backend: a small server function that is rate-limited, has a daily cap and falls back to a backup model.

22. A second app: a Flask viewer with an observation timeline and a Gaia overlay.

23. Verification tools:

  • verify_releases.py
  • validate_targets.py
  • retry_benchmark.py

24. Documentation: data sources, verification, testing, index rebuilds and the assistant.
